overview.text:
Mahabaleshwar sits at about 4,500 ft on a plateau in the Sahyadris and is two places in one. Old Mahabaleshwar is a pilgrimage centre: the Krishna and five tributaries rise here, and the 500-year-old Mahabaleshwar temple has a self-originated lingam and a gold platform given by Shivaji. Under the British, New Mahabaleshwar became the summer capital of the Bombay Presidency.

Today it is Maharashtra's favourite hill retreat. Viewpoints such as Arthur's Seat look over the Deccan and Konkan, Venna Lake has boating, and strawberry season fills the streets with shakes and jams. Pratapgad Fort, built by Shivaji in 1665, is close by, Panchgani is 20 km away, and Kaas Pathar's wildflower plateau is within reach. The monsoon is very wet.

how_to_reach.text:
By air: Pune airport is about 120 km away; Mumbai airport is 270 km.

By train: the nearest railway station is Satara, 60 km away; Pune station is about 120 km.

By road: state buses run from Satara and Pune.

best_time.text: The monsoon is very heavy, with 10–12 days of continuous rain in July most years, so plan for wet roads and misty viewpoints then. Strawberry season brings fruit stalls everywhere, and the Strawberry Fair at Mapro Gardens falls on the Easter weekend.

overview.text:
Lonavala and Khandala are twin hill stations about 5 km apart in the Sahyadri range, at around 622 m, on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway. Lord Elphinstone, Governor of Bombay, set them up as hill stations in 1871. Today they are the weekend escape for both cities: about 64 km from Pune and 96 km from Mumbai.

The monsoon is peak season, when the hills turn green and waterfalls run off every slope; viewpoints such as Tiger's Leap and Duke's Nose drop away to the valleys below. History is close too: the 2nd-century BCE Buddhist caves of Karla and Bhaja, and the Maratha forts of Lohagad, Visapur and Rajmachi. Take home chikki, the jaggery-and-peanut candy the town is famous for. In the rains, stay well away from fast water at the dams and falls.

how_to_reach.text:
By train: Lonavala is a major stop between Mumbai and Pune. Local trains run from Pune every two hours, and Mumbai is about 2.5 hours by train; Mumbai suburban trains end at Khopoli, 15 km away, with buses on.

By road: about 64 km from Pune and 96 km from Mumbai on the Mumbai–Pune Expressway.

By air: Pune (64 km), Navi Mumbai (65 km) or Mumbai (104 km).

best_time.text: The monsoon, June to September, is the peak season: very wet, intensely green and full of waterfalls, but crowded and slippery. Mid-October to May is dry, better for trekking the forts and visiting the caves in comfort.

overview.text:
The Karla Caves are a group of Buddhist rock-cut shrines about 10.9 km from Lonavala, cut into the hillside over several centuries, from the 2nd century BCE to the 5th century CE. They stood near an ancient trade route running from the Arabian Sea into the Deccan.

Their glory is the Grand Chaitya, Cave 8: the largest and most completely preserved chaitya hall of its period, a long vaulted prayer hall lined with sculpted pillars and lit by a great window cut into the rock. Combine it with the Bhaja Caves on the other side of the valley.

overview.text: The Bhaja Caves are a group of 22 Buddhist rock-cut caves from the 2nd century BC, set about 400 ft above Bhaja village on an old trade route. They are about 2 km from Malavli station, near Lonavala, and are usually combined with Karla and the trek up Lohagad.

overview.text: Lohagad is a hill fort rising to 1,033 m, about 20 km from Lonavala, just south-west of the larger Visapur fort. It is one of the most popular treks in the area, starting near Malavli, and is often combined with the Bhaja Caves on the way. The trail gets slippery in the monsoon.
